speaker: Doctor
text:
I am Dr. Agent. You are here for wrist pain and difficulty moving your hand; can you tell me exactly where the pain is located and if it started after an injury or gradually?

To help me narrow this down, does the pain get worse when you try to grip something, turn a doorknob, or lift a cup? Also, have you noticed any swelling, redness, or a specific click or pop when you move your wrist?

speaker: Patient
text: 34-year-old female. The patient reports experiencing pain in her right thumb and wrist, which radiates to her elbow for the past three months. The pain worsens when she holds her infant son and is alleviated somewhat with an ice pack. She mentions a history of falling on her right outstretched hand about six months ago. She also notes that her mother has a history of chronic joint pain treated with methotrexate. The patient has been taking ibuprofen as needed for her symptoms.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: De Quervain's tenosynovitis. The patient's history of repetitive gripping (holding an infant), localized pain at the thumb base radiating to the wrist, and relief with ice are classic signs of stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment. While the fall six months ago may have contributed to initial tenderness, the persistent activity-related symptoms and maternal history of inflammatory arthritis suggest an overuse component potentially exacerbated by underlying susceptibility. I will recommend a focused physical exam (Finkelstein's test) and consider a corticosteroid injection if conservative management with ice and activity modification fails.
